note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1254) — Trace one hanging spikelet to its long stalk. The Flora describes drooping branches and flattened spikelets 6–20 mm wide.

Follow an arching panicle branch to ONE flattened, many-flowered spikelet, commonly 20–40 mm long, hanging from a slender roughly 10–30 mm pedicel. Each overlapping pointed scale is principally a FLORET lemma, not an individual seed. Green and mature tan forms are both pictured; neither color alone is diagnostic.
tiles.short: Large flat fish-shaped spikelets dangling on long stalks
tiles.status: VISIBLE ON REAL PHOTOS; SCALE-SPECIFIC SAME-PLANT CHECK PENDING

tiles.heading: 02 · FOLLOW THE PLANT TO ITS BASE
tiles.details: This woodland and riparian perennial has short, stout, scaly rhizomes and often 8–20 mm wide flat bamboo-like leaf blades. The existing rhizome plate shows actual connected basal shoots and roots, but not one continuous flowering culm attached to that same underground base. Do not mistake a broadleaf sedge for this grass when sterile.
tiles.short: Perennial with broad leaves and short rhizomes
tiles.status: ROOTSTOCK PHOTO PRESENT; SAME-PLANT FLOWERING CONNECTION MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT THE SPIKELET, THEN THE GLUMES
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1254) — Start at the base of one flat spikelet and count upward. The regional key gives usually 6–17 florets, occasionally up to 26.

One laterally flattened 20–40 mm spikelet generally contains about 6–17 florets (treatment ranges vary). The TWO short outer basal glumes are commonly 5–7 mm and should be distinguished from the one or two reduced sterile lemmas and the many larger overlapping fertile lemmas. Current intact-spikelet photos do NOT prove a separately dissected, individually arrow-verified pair of glumes.

Use the green spikelet to follow the overlapping florets. Photo still needed: a scaled view with the two small basal glumes separated from the florets.
tiles.short: 6–17 florets; two small basal glumes about 5–7 mm
tiles.status: PUBLISHED MEASUREMENTS; DETACHED GLUME PHOTO GAP

tiles.heading: 04 · OPEN A TRUE FLORET
tiles.details: Fertile lemmas are broad, strongly keeled, many-veined (often 11–15 veins in regional treatments) and approximately 6–12 mm long; they are pointed but lack conspicuous long awns. A palea and actual grain/caryopsis lie INSIDE a fertile floret. Existing dissection photographs show real separated bracts and grain, but do not justify labeling any loose part a basal glume.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma roughly 6–12 mm; no long awn
tiles.status: FLORET DISSECTION VISIBLE; GLUME/LEMMA SCALE QA PENDING

tiles.heading: 05 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: Separate blade from sheath and examine the inner junction at 10–20× with a 1-mm ruler. A short, jagged to minutely ciliate membranous ligule is expected, approximately 0.7 mm in the UT Williamson County treatment. The current collar photo locates the junction but its true membrane tip is NOT clear enough for a precise arrow or independent measurement.

tiles.heading: 06 · RULE OUT SMALL WOODOATS
tiles.details: C. laxum and C. sessiliflorum usually have much smaller, often about 4–10 mm spikelets on short stalks, not the conspicuous 20–40 mm long-pedicelled hanging fish of inland sea oats. Existing comparison panels show other source-labelled taxa but are not matched at the same scale or verified as Hays vouchers. Finalize only after rights, anatomy arrows, and actual public-page QA pass.
tiles.short: Other Chasmanthium have much smaller, short-stalked units
tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE LESSON; MATCHED LOCAL MACRO + SITE QA GAP

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: INLAND SEA OATS — look for large fish-shaped HANGING SPIKELETS on long thin pedicels under broad bamboo-like leaves. Follow the genuine live panicle in Bob Harms CHLA5-I; CHLA5-J isolates ONE actual many-flowered flattened green SPIKELET. Each overlapping pointed shield is a FLORET LEMMA, not one loose grass seed. CHLA5-j1 shows the dry hanging stage, CHLA5-J2 an actual yellowish pollen-bearing ANTHER in an opened floret, CHLA5-9 separates enclosing floral scales and TRUE DARK CARYOPSIS, and CHLA5-8 reveals actual scaly shallow rhizome and attached root crowns. Examine CHLA5-L for the attached blade–sheath collar; the minute ~0.7mm membranous ligule margin is NOT independently arrow-worthy from that photograph. Compare C. laxum and sessiliflorum tiny much shorter stalked spikelets without making new county nativity assertions.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: This woodland and riparian perennial has short, stout, scaly rhizomes and often 8–20 mm wide flat bamboo-like leaf blades. The existing rhizome plate shows actual connected basal shoots and roots, but not one continuous flowering culm attached to that same underground base. Do not mistake a broadleaf sedge for this grass when sterile.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: One laterally flattened 20–40 mm spikelet generally contains about 6–17 florets (treatment ranges vary). The TWO short outer basal glumes are commonly 5–7 mm and should be distinguished from the one or two reduced sterile lemmas and the many larger overlapping fertile lemmas. Current intact-spikelet photos do NOT prove a separately dissected, individually arrow-verified pair of glumes.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: C. latifolium has LARGE ~20–40 mm spikelets on LONG 10–30 mm dangling pedicels; C. laxum and C. sessiliflorum have much smaller short-stalked spikelets and generally narrower/ascending heads. Coastal Uniola paniculata and nodding Briza also have flat spikelets but differ in genus, inflorescence and habitat. Use morphology rather than a common name or habitat alone.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: Broadleaf Woodoats — flat spikelets hanging from slender stalks
panels.caption: A genuine attached inland sea oats panicle. Follow the slender overhead arching flowering axis: many separate flat, fish-shaped SPIKELETS hang beneath it on fine stalks. Each 'fish' is one MANY-FLORETED spikelet—not a single seed or an individual floret. This clear whole-head photo is useful alongside its rooted green basal habit image.
panels.creator: Douglas Goldman

panels.label: ACTUAL LEAF COLLAR — blade joining the green sheath
panels.caption: The broad green leaf blade angles away from a narrow upright grass culm. The actual BLADE–SHEATH junction lies where that blade attaches; the sheath continues down the stem below. We can point to the visible collar area. We CANNOT call the small pale surface a photographed true ligule membrane or measure its toothed margin from this photograph; a 10–20× inner-collar view with scale is still required.

panels.label: GROWTH BASE IN HABITAT — living basal green leaves from woodland litter
panels.caption: Douglas Goldman photographed actual living inland sea oats near ground level in a South Carolina bottomland woodland. Broad, slightly folded green blades emerge from overlapping basal sheaths among dead leaves. This records what the BASE looks like in habitat, NOT an exposed rhizome, connected underground runner or individually dissected rooted crown. For the true shallow rhizome, compare the separate Bob Harms anatomical view only under its credited educational-use permission.

panels.label: Broadleaf Woodoats — overlapping florets on one intact spikelet

Unlike the first Jim Conrad source photo, this is a separate copyright holder Gaiacoyote public-domain photograph. Mississippi, not a local Hays voucher.

intro: INLAND SEA OATS — look for large fish-shaped HANGING SPIKELETS on long thin pedicels under broad bamboo-like leaves. Follow the genuine live panicle in Bob Harms CHLA5-I; CHLA5-J isolates ONE actual many-flowered flattened green SPIKELET. Each overlapping pointed shield is a FLORET LEMMA, not one loose grass seed. CHLA5-j1 shows the dry hanging stage, CHLA5-J2 an actual yellowish pollen-bearing ANTHER in an opened floret, CHLA5-9 separates enclosing floral scales and TRUE DARK CARYOPSIS, and CHLA5-8 reveals actual scaly shallow rhizome and attached root crowns. Examine CHLA5-L for the attached blade–sheath collar; the minute ~0.7mm membranous ligule margin is NOT independently arrow-worthy from that photograph. Compare C. laxum and sessiliflorum tiny much shorter stalked spikelets without making new county nativity assertions.
memory_rule: INLAND = BIG MANY-FLORETED FLAT 'FISH' 20–40 mm on LONG slender PEDICELS. C. LAXUM and C. SESSILIFLORUM = generally smaller, much shorter-stalked spikelets, narrower/contracted heads. The tiny ligule is at the blade–sheath collar. Two small basal GLUMES are not the repeated large LEMMAS.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: C. latifolium has LARGE ~20–40 mm spikelets on LONG 10–30 mm dangling pedicels; C. laxum and C. sessiliflorum have much smaller short-stalked spikelets and generally narrower/ascending heads. Coastal Uniola paniculata and nodding Briza also have flat spikelets but differ in genus, inflorescence and habitat. Use morphology rather than a common name or habitat alone.
